extracted.intended_audience: Department of Defense medical managers, health care productivity analysts, policy makers responsible for workload measurement and resource allocation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critique on constructing and using the Health Care Unit (HCU) and Composite Work Unit (CWU) as output/workload measures for military medical facilities, including methods to compute weights, regression formulations, inflation adjustments, and cautions about use for resource allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 25 Performance Factors to define outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Health Care Unit is composed by utilizing the 25 Performance Factors which cover all of the gross products (i.e., medical, surgical, etc.) being produced in military health care facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The HCU partitions inpatient care into separate categories, apportions outpatient and dental care into categories, and ties expense of providing care into a single index. This composition is intended to reflect a more comprehensive view of hospital products and be effective for large systems (Ref. 26: p. 732).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute weights as normalized fixed and variable cost ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Weights for performance factors can be computed by dividing fixed and variable cost components by the average fiscal year cost per disposition (e.g., Wx = fixed_cost/average_cost_per_disposition, Wy = variable_cost/average_cost_per_disposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For a Category I facility, Wx = 329.30/990.44 = .332 where 329.30 is fixed cost ($/disp) and 990.44 is average fiscal year cost per disposition. This method apportions 'credit' for each inpatient stay among the corresponding performance factor weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid peer-group-specific weights; prefer a common weight set
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not compute different weights by peer group because peer-group weights are likely to confuse inefficiency with case mix complexity; users preferred all hospitals use the same set of weights to simplify application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refined study deleted peer groupings because weights computed by peer group gave increased value for certain types of care in smaller, less complex facilities than the same care in large facilities, thereby rewarding inefficiency (Ref. 29: pp. 3-4; Ref. 27: pp. 6-7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive inpatient weights using middle-50% subsample (exclude upper/lower quartiles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute bed day and disposition weights from a subsample consisting of the middle fifty percent of the sample by number of dispositions after eliminating upper and lower quartiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces outlier influence. For each Uniform Chart of Accounts Summary Account perform regression on the subsample to obtain coefficients B0 and B1, then apply the linear equation EXP/DISP = B0(DIS P) + B1(LOS) (with inflation adjustments) to compute weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use regression (EXP/DISP = B0*DISP + B1*LOS) to obtain cost coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: For each inpatient summary account, perform linear regression on the subsample to obtain coefficients B0 and B1 where EXP = total summary account expense, DISP = total dispositions, LOS = average length of stay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because parameters vary with cost inflation, include additional parameters (dummy-year inflation factors) when applying coefficients across years (see inflation-adjusted formulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust regression coefficients for hospital cost inflation
rubrics_metrics.description: The regression equation should include inflation adjustment parameters (k1, k2 with year dummies) so that EXP/DISP = (B0 + B1*LOS) + (1 + k1*d(yr1)) + k2*d(yr2) to allow use of base-year coefficients across fiscal years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: k1 and k2 represent levels of hospital inflation; dummy variables d(yr1) take value 1 for fiscal year 1981, etc., enabling a base year regression to be adjusted for subsequent years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute outpatient and dental weights relative to inpatient disposition cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Outpatient and dental weights are computed for each account as fiscal year cost per account divided by average fiscal year cost per disposition, i.e., W = FY cost per account / average FY cost per disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses the value of one outpatient clinic visit in relation to one average inpatient disposition; outpatient weights are generally small (e.g., .030 or less) meaning 10 to 30 outpatient visits equal one inpatient stay (Ref. 29: p. A3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer dispositions rather than occupied bed days as inpatient input
rubrics_metrics.description: Using dispositions (admissions) as the only inpatient input factor was recommended because each disposition should represent a fixed sum of occupied bed days and reflect expected length-of-stay bounds for diagnoses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occupied bed days are manipulable and may discourage shortening lengths of stay. However, DRG approaches that use length-of-stay elements also have limitations (geographic/demographic variation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust measures for case-mix intensity, complexity, and severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Productivity measures must recognize differences in service-mix and case-mix (intensity, complexity, severity) so that weights reflect resource requirements by illness severity rather than treating patients as homogeneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The HCU (as developed) and the CWU were criticized as ineffective in assigning proper weights according to severity and resource requirement and thus inappropriate for intra/inter-Service productivity comparisons (Navy non-concurrence, Ref. 27).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume uniform quality of care across facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: When viewing inputs as 'products' an assumption is often made that all care provided is quality care as established by standards; this is problematic because correct diagnosis, appropriate diagnostic studies, therapies, and physician competence vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures should not implicitly assume all outputs are equivalent in quality; quality variation must be considered or measures will misrepresent productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and adjust for non-quantifiable functions (training, standby, emergency readiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: HCU/CWU computations do not directly measure non-measurable but important functions such as contingency standby capabilities, emergency room readiness, or training/research duties of staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large tertiary facilities provide training and research that generate workload differently; failure to account for these functions underestimates the resource needs and mission requirements of such facilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require consistent and accurate Uniform Chart of Accounts data and allocation procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Uniform Chart of Accounts must provide factual and accurate expense and workload data, but variability in cost pool allocation procedures across facilities undermines consistency of HCU computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final account expenses may not be under the management control of the service chief; many different allocation procedures for cost pools provide minimal consistency and reduce comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using outputs that are actually inputs or intermediate outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful that chosen 'output' measures are not in fact inputs or intermediate outputs (e.g., occupied bed days) which are subject to manipulation if tied to resource allocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report warns that many output measures used are really inputs or intermediate outputs and thus subject to manipulation; accurate, consistent measures of true output are crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish standards or benchmarks for costs used to derive weights
rubrics_metrics.description: Weights are based on historical expenses, but no standards are established for what these costs should be; without benchmarks it's unclear whether average disposition costs are reasonable across DOD or civilian comparators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions such as whether a DoD average disposition cost of $1000 vs. civilian $750 are reasonable must be addressed before HCU can serve as a valid productivity index or resource allocator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design measures to minimize perverse incentives that distort service mix
rubrics_metrics.description: When weights give higher value to certain types of care (e.g., orthopedic, surgical), measures may incentivize admitting or classifying patients into higher-weight categories to inflate productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The HCU could make higher-weight services more desirable, leading to manipulation (admit patients to orthopedic service when medical admission is appropriate) and shifts in staffing priorities that distort care provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor total- or multi-factor productivity measurement over single-factor measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying on partial or single-factor productivity measures (like labor productivity/CWU/FTE) is inadequate; total resource or partial-factor measures should be considered to reflect influences beyond labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DoD overemphasizes direct labor productivity; since outputs cannot be wholly explained by labor, management should pursue total factor measurement and avoid single-factor illusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure data quality, comprehensiveness, and accuracy for usable trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Productivity data submitted to statistical agencies must be suitable, comprehensive, and accurate; flawed data make productivity trends meaningless without extensive qualification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts noted the submitted productivity data were so flawed as to be useless without extensive analysis; issues include suitability of output measures, comprehensiveness, and accuracy of source data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow demographic/geographic adjustment when applying length-of-stay standards (DRG comparisons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Length-of-stay norms derived in one geographic area (or DRG set) do not necessarily apply elsewhere; adjustments for local demographic conditions are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A study found DRGs established for New Jersey did not apply to patients in Pennsylvania or Ohio, indicating need to adjust lengths of stay by demographic/geographic factors (Ref. 30: pp. 50-51).

rubrics_metrics.name: If used for resource allocation, incorporate hospital-specific weighting or adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of wide ranges and variability in indices across hospitals, using HCU for allocation would require an equation that utilizes a weight for each individual hospital; otherwise allocation is impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer-group study showed wide ranges in dollars/HCU, HCU per physician, HCU/FTE, and HCU/OB; extreme outliers were discarded but ranges remain wide making allocation without hospital-specific adjustments extremely difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate productivity program elements: measurement, identification, resource provision
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful productivity program combines (1) productivity measurement, (2) identification of new ways to improve productivity, and (3) provision of resources necessary to implement improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three elements must be integrated so management can observe efficiency, identify opportunities for improvement, and commit management, capital, and employees to realistic achievement targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require components to support productivity projections or accept alternative projections
rubrics_metrics.description: Components that cannot show productivity improvements or cannot support projected productivity changes in budgets may have alternative projections made by OMB/OSD based on other factors (investments, workload changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DODI 5010.34 warns components not demonstrating productivity improvements or supporting projections may find OMB/OSD making alternative projections (Ref. 8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide ability to compare absolute efficiency across similar facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures should permit comparison of absolute efficiency of one medical care entity to another of similar product and size; CWU/FTE index does not readily permit such absolute comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-factor indices like CWU/FTE express performance over time but are poor for cross-sectional comparisons because they fail to reflect inputs other than labor and differences in case mix.
